paras: The threatened lynching of Embry, Johnson and Hanesford took place on the night of Saturday, 1 August 1885, when a mob planned to take three Black prisoners from the jail at Stanford, Lincoln County, Kentucky, and hang them. After a delegation of Black men offered to guard the jail, Judge Varnon had the sheriff and jailer take the prisoners away, and no one was harmed. The Stanford Interior Journal, the only paper found to name the prisoners, used the episode to condemn mob violence against prisoners already held by the law.

The three prisoners, identified only by surname and described as "negro boys," were held in the Stanford jail "charged with detaining the Misses Marcum against their will." According to the Interior Journal, they had given themselves away on returning to town by telling, in the presence of an officer, what they had done.

On the same Saturday night a mob set out for Danville to hang a Black prisoner named Anderson, accused of an assault on Mrs. J. H. Hiatt. The Interior Journal put that mob at "probably a hundred strong" and said its plans failed because most of its members "could not keep their counsel"; the Danville jailer, warned of its coming, had hidden Anderson in the court-house.

When it was learned that Saturday night that the mob also intended to hang the prisoners at Stanford, a delegation of 25 or 30 "leading colored men" called on Judge Varnon and volunteered to guard the jail. Fearing that their presence at the jail might cause further trouble, the judge declined and instead ordered Sheriff Menefee and Jailer Newland to take the prisoners away. The paper also passed on a report that others in town meant to use a jail break-in to free Bill Carson and to kill "the negro boy, Rusty Welch."
No attack on the Stanford jail is reported. The coverage does not say where the prisoners were taken, and no later report of their case, an arrest of mob members or a trial was found.

Three days later the Interior Journal returned to the Danville mob, reporting that some of its members had stopped two boys on the pike and tried to tie one of them to a fence, which it offered as proof that "no good citizen should ever encourage a mob spirit."

The Interior Journal, Stanford's own paper, carried the episode in two items of its 4 August local column. It praised Jailer Newland as an officer who would defend his prisoners, and it argued that the case did not demand mob violence, "especially since they are in the hands of the law," reminding readers that "it is as much murder for a hundred persons to kill a man as if one alone did it." The same paragraph called two of the prisoners "pretty mean negroes" who deserved to be severely punished.

Outside Kentucky the story appeared only as a one-line item in news columns, in the Belmont Chronicle of St. Clairsville, Ohio, on 6 August and the Asheville Citizen on 18 August. These briefs stated as fact that a single unnamed "negro in jail at Stanford" had made "a brutal assault upon the wife of a respectable merchant," a "farmer" in the Asheville version. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The local paper and the out-of-state briefs disagree on both the number of prisoners and the charge: three boys accused of detaining two girls, against one man accused of assaulting a married woman. The briefs' version more closely matches the Interior Journal's account of the Anderson case, though Anderson was held at Danville rather than Stanford, so they may describe that case rather than this one.

bases: A mob planned to take three jailed Black prisoners from the Stanford jail and hang them, but officials removed the prisoners and no one was harmed (A1).

The mob intended to hang the prisoners, who were charged with detaining two white girls, but the prisoners were removed from the jail and no killing is reported (A1); this was a threatened lynching only.

Only the Stanford Interior Journal reports the threat against the named prisoners (A1); the out-of-state briefs describe a single prisoner and a different accusation and may concern another case (A3, A5).

accounts.label: Local paper (Stanford Interior Journal)
accounts.gist: On Saturday night the mob bound for Danville also meant to hang the three jailed boys; Black men offered to guard the jail and the judge had the prisoners removed instead.

accounts.label: Out-of-state news brief
accounts.gist: A single unnamed negro in jail at Stanford was threatened with lynching for a brutal assault on the wife of a respectable merchant (or farmer).

framing.detail: The Interior Journal opposed mob violence against prisoners 'in the hands of the law' and warned that a mob killing is murder, while calling two prisoners 'pretty mean negroes' who deserved severe punishment.
Ohio and North Carolina news columns gave a one-line brief stating the alleged assault as fact.

H. Hiatt), whose would-be lynchers went to Danville, so the briefs may concern that case.
